article.plain_text:
In Part One, we introduced CRISPR and its limitations. Conventional CRISPR-Cas9 editing produces a double-strand break in DNA whose repair can leave several different genetic changes. Following that break, one common response is non-homologous end joining, which reconnects the broken DNA ends without requiring a supplied repair template. The process can restore the original sequence, although processing of the ends can also introduce small insertions or deletions, collectively called indels. When an indel disrupts a gene’s function, the result can be a gene knockout. Such knockouts have allowed researchers to create animal models and investigate what happens when a particular gene loses its function. [1]
Restoring gene function, on the other hand, can require correcting an existing mutation or introducing functional DNA through a knock-in, a targeted insertion of a specified sequence. Researchers can attempt this by supplying a DNA template that carries the desired change between stretches matching the chromosome on either side. Through homology-directed repair, or HDR, the cell can copy that change into its own DNA as it repairs the double-strand break. [1]
However, supplying the template does not ensure that the cell will use it. HDR competes with other repair pathways, and its efficiency depends on the cell type and state, including whether the cell is dividing. Many cells relevant to treatment, such as mature neurons, are difficult to edit efficiently through this route. The double-strand break can also produce large deletions or rearrangements of chromosome material, even when Cas9 has recognized the intended target. [1]
To overcome some of these limitations, researchers have developed editing methods that build on CRISPR’s targeting system. Base editing combines that targeting system with enzymes that chemically convert individual DNA bases without requiring a double-strand break. [2] [3]
A base substitution replaces one of DNA’s four chemical bases, adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) or thymine (T), with another. Across the double helix, A pairs with T and C pairs with G. If a C is changed to a T on one strand, the complementary strand must eventually change from G to A for the two strands to agree. A permanent C-to-T substitution can therefore also be described as a G-to-A substitution when the same DNA is read from the opposite strand. [2] [3]
In a base editor, a deaminase is attached to a modified Cas9 protein. A deaminase is an enzyme that removes an amino group from a base, changing its chemical structure and how it pairs with other bases. Cas9 and its guide RNA position this enzyme at the desired sequence. As the guide pairs with one DNA strand, a short stretch of the opposite strand becomes exposed and available for the attached enzyme to act on. [2] [3]
The first cytosine base editors, reported by Alexis Komor and colleagues in Liu’s laboratory in 2016, use a deaminase to convert C into uracil, a base normally found in RNA that pairs like thymine. This creates a uracil-G mismatch within the DNA. The cell can remove uracil and reverse the intended change, so the researchers added a component that inhibits the enzyme responsible for initiating its removal. They also adapted Cas9 to nick the opposite, unedited DNA strand, breaking only one of the two backbones. That nick encourages repair to replace the unedited strand using the chemically altered strand as its template. Subsequent processing can turn the original C-G pair into a stable T-A pair. [3]
Adenine base editors apply a related strategy to A-to-G substitutions. Their deaminase produces inosine-containing DNA, which the cell’s copying machinery reads like guanine, and repair can convert the original A-T pair into a G-C pair. Developing this editor required an enzyme with a new activity. At the time, no natural enzyme was known to perform the required adenine deamination in DNA. Nicole Gaudelli and colleagues began with a bacterial enzyme that modifies RNA and used laboratory evolution and protein engineering to develop versions that could act on DNA. Their work, published in 2017, added A-to-G and T-to-C changes to the C-to-T and G-to-A changes available from cytosine editors. [4]
Each of the four DNA bases could, in principle, be replaced by any of the other three, giving twelve possible single-base substitutions. The original cytosine and adenine editors enable changes, or corrections for four of those substitutions. A mutation requiring an A-to-T correction, for example, cannot be directly corrected through their C-to-T or A-to-G chemistry. Converting bases alone also cannot insert a missing DNA segment or remove an unwanted insertion. [1] [2]
Even when the required conversion is available, the surrounding sequence affects how cleanly it can be made. The deaminase acts within a short editing window, and several susceptible bases within that window can be modified together. Correcting one cytosine could therefore alter another nearby cytosine that should have been preserved. These additional changes are called bystander edits. Their consequences depend on where they occur, such as whether they change another amino acid in the resulting protein. Researchers can alter the enzyme’s editing window or choose another guide to improve the outcome, although guide placement must also satisfy Cas9’s requirement for a neighboring recognition sequence, the protospacer adjacent motif, or PAM. [1] [2]
Off-target editing presents another limitation because the Cas9-guide complex can recognize similar DNA sequences elsewhere in the genome. Some deaminases can also modify DNA or RNA independently of where the guide directs Cas9. These activities vary between editor versions, and engineering can reduce particular unwanted reactions. [1] [2]
Despite these limitations, base editing has produced substantial improvements in experimental disease models. Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome causes severe premature aging and commonly results from a C-to-T mutation in LMNA, the gene that supplies the lamin A protein. Lamin A helps support the nucleus, and the mutation changes how the cell splices the gene’s RNA. During normal splicing, sections called introns are removed and the retained exons are joined to form the mature message. The progeria mutation creates an inappropriate splice site that removes part of the lamin A instructions, producing a shortened protein called progerin that disrupts nuclear structure and function. [1] [5]
An adenine base editor can reverse this mutation by changing the A opposite the mutated T into a base that is read as G, allowing repair processes to restore the original C-G pair. Luke Koblan and colleagues tested this approach in cells from children with progeria and in mice carrying the human disease mutation. Correction in the patient-derived cells reduced the abnormal RNA and progerin protein and improved nuclear shape. For the animal experiments, the researchers delivered genetic instructions for the editor using modified viruses. A single treatment at two weeks of age preserved smooth muscle cells in the aorta, the major artery leaving the heart. The ten treated mice had a median lifespan of 510 days, compared with 215 days for twelve saline-treated controls. [5]
Another development of CRISPR’s targeting system is prime editing, which uses an RNA template to let researchers specify virtually any replacement DNA sequence within the system’s edit-length limits. The sequence is supplied as information to be copied, allowing the correction to include substitutions, insertions and deletions beyond the chemical conversions available to the original base editors. Andrew Anzalone and colleagues first reported this approach in 2019. [2] [6]
To write the specified sequence, a prime editor combines a Cas9 nickase with an engineered reverse transcriptase. The nickase introduces a single-strand break, and the reverse transcriptase extends the resulting DNA end by copying an RNA template. Reverse transcription is also used in single-cell RNA sequencing to turn captured RNA into DNA suitable for sequencing. In prime editing, the newly copied DNA is attached directly to the chromosome being edited. [1] [6]
The prime-editing guide RNA, or pegRNA, provides both targeting and copying instructions. It retains the part of a CRISPR guide that recognizes the chosen DNA site and adds an extension with two further functions. One portion binds the DNA end exposed by the nick, providing a starting point for copying. The other carries the template containing the desired edit. Once the DNA end has paired with the pegRNA, the attached reverse transcriptase can extend it by copying that template. [1] [6]
This produces an extended DNA segment, often called a flap, that contains the edit and remains attached to the chromosome. The extension can pair with matching DNA on the opposite strand and displace the original segment. Cellular enzymes can then remove the displaced original DNA and join the newly written sequence into place. At this stage, the double helix contains one edited strand and one unedited strand, and further repair can make both strands retain the change. Some prime-editing systems introduce another nick in the unedited strand to encourage the cell to replace it using the edited strand as a template. [1] [6]
The template can encode any of the twelve types of single-base substitution, as well as small insertions, deletions and combinations of these changes. Conventional prime editing does not require a separate donor DNA molecule because the sequence to be copied is already contained in the pegRNA. Its practical reach depends on the length and structure of that template, the available target sites and the ability of the editor and cell to complete the reaction. [1] [2] [6]
One limitation is that the pegRNA must remain intact long enough to supply its template. Cellular enzymes can degrade its exposed extension, leaving shortened guides that still bind the editor or target DNA without being able to support productive copying. These incomplete guides can also occupy proteins and target sites that intact guides would otherwise use. To address this, researchers in Liu’s laboratory added compact RNA structures that protect the extension from degradation. The resulting engineered pegRNAs increased editing efficiency in the tested human cell lines and patient-derived fibroblasts. [1]
The cellular response also affects whether the new DNA is retained. Mismatch repair normally helps correct disagreements between the two DNA strands, and it can recognize a prime-editing intermediate as something that needs correction. If it removes the newly written strand before that strand has been sealed into place, the original sequence is restored. Temporarily inhibiting this response has improved editing in laboratory experiments. Unwanted indels can also still arise during processing, particularly in systems that nick both strands, where concurrent nicks can sometimes result in a double-strand break. [1] [6] [7]
Larger sequence replacements introduce another challenge because prime editing initially writes the new sequence onto one DNA strand. The new segment must then be incorporated and its information retained across both strands. Twin prime editing extends this approach by using two pegRNAs to write complementary new sequences onto opposite strands. Those newly written segments can pair with each other, allowing cellular enzymes to remove the original intervening DNA and join the new segments into the chromosome. This arrangement can replace larger stretches without first copying the edit from one strand onto the other. [1] [8]
Twin prime editing can also prepare a target for another enzyme. Researchers can use it to install a short recognition sequence for a recombinase, an enzyme that joins DNA at particular sites. A separately supplied DNA molecule carries a corresponding recognition site and the larger sequence to be inserted. The recombinase then joins that cargo to the prepared genomic site. Combining these systems has enabled gene-sized insertions in cultured human cells. For diseases caused by different loss-of-function mutations in the same gene, inserting a functional sequence could offer a way to address several mutations with one general approach. It also adds a recombinase and donor DNA to the material that must enter the cell. [1] [2] [8]
That leads into an obvious question, which is, given these powerful tools for programming the genome, why do so many genetic diseases remain difficult to treat? Among the reasons is the difficulty of delivering an editor to enough of the cells responsible for a disease. Addressability is one of the three pillars of any framework for thinking about therapeutic development and progress, alongside observability and programmability.
Observability concerns our ability to measure cellular function and disease. Single-cell RNA sequencing, for instance, has expanded that ability by distinguishing RNA profiles among individual cells, although those profiles remain partial measurements of a dynamic system. [10] Programmability concerns the biological changes that we can specify and induce, and base and prime editing techniques covered here significantly expand this capability by allowing researchers to prescribe particular changes to DNA. Addressability concerns the cells in which those changes can actually be made, and reaching target cells with these large biomolecular therapies remains perhaps the greatest underappreciated challenge of the three.
For base and prime editing, the therapeutic cargo includes an editing protein and its guide RNA. Researchers can deliver the assembled complex directly or supply genetic instructions for the cell to produce the protein, which must then bind to its guide RNA. DNA instructions must first reach the nucleus and be transcribed into messenger RNA, which the cell then translates into the editing protein. Supplying messenger RNA bypasses transcription and allows the cell to begin with protein production. [11] [12]
Whichever form is used, the editor must reach enough of the cells responsible for disease to produce a therapeutic effect. The guide RNA recognizes a DNA sequence that may be shared by many cell types, so its sequence specificity does not itself direct the cargo to the tissue that needs treatment. Delivery must therefore bring the cargo into that tissue and its target cells. During uptake, cells can enclose the material within membrane-bound compartments called endosomes, from which it must escape before the editing protein and guide RNA can gain access to nuclear DNA. [11] [12]
One way around much of the distribution problem is to remove the target cells for editing outside the body, or ex vivo. For instance, blood-forming stem cells normally replenish the blood throughout life and can be collected for treatment under laboratory conditions. Techniques such as electroporation use electrical pulses to help introduce editing material into those cells. Researchers can then examine the resulting genetic changes and cellular behavior before returning the cells to the patient. If the edited stem cells successfully settle into the bone marrow and continue functioning there, they can supply new blood cells carrying the modification. [11] [12]
For cells that must remain in place, treatment requires delivery inside the body, or in vivo. Mature neurons illustrate the difficulty because they are embedded in existing tissue and connected to other cells through established circuits. Removing them for editing and returning them would require reestablishing those relationships. Delivery through the circulation also encounters the blood-brain barrier, where the properties of the brain’s blood vessels restrict the passage of many substances into the tissue. Direct injection can provide access to a local region, although the editor must still spread far enough to reach the required neuronal population. [11] [16]
Carrying the editing machinery into tissues therefore requires a delivery vehicle suited to the cargo and target. Two widely used approaches are lipid nanoparticles, which package material within lipid-based particles, and viral vectors, which adapt viruses’ ability to enter cells and transfer genetic material. Their behavior in the body determines which organs and cell populations receive the cargo, and how much of it becomes available inside those cells. [11] [12]
Lipid nanoparticles can carry messenger RNA encoding an editor together with its guide RNA. After uptake and release of the RNA, the cell produces the editing protein, creating a temporary supply that eventually disappears as the RNA and protein degrade. A successfully installed DNA change can persist after this exposure ends. Many nanoparticle formulations accumulate in the liver following administration through the bloodstream, making that organ relatively accessible to editing. This helps explain the prominence of liver targets among early in vivo applications. [12]
Viral vectors provide another route into cells. Adeno-associated virus, or AAV, has been adapted into a delivery vector whose protein shell carries DNA instructions for a therapeutic product. In gene augmentation, those instructions can supply a functional gene. For gene editing, they can instead encode the machinery that changes a sequence already present in the cell. Researchers can choose or engineer the AAV shell, called its capsid, and alter the administration route to influence which tissues receive the material. The viral components needed for replication are removed from the therapeutic vector, so the treated cells do not produce a spreading viral infection. [11] [12]
Once AAV is chosen, its cargo capacity constrains what can be delivered. A typical prime editor’s encoding sequence, for instance, is too large for the roughly 4,700-base capacity of one AAV vector. Researchers have therefore used techniques like splitting instructions between two vectors and arranging for the resulting protein parts to reassemble inside the cell. [13]
Delivering the editor’s DNA instructions by AAV also affects how long the cell produces it. AAV-delivered DNA can remain active for a long time, which is useful when the treatment supplies a missing protein. For gene editing however, this persistence can maintain production after the intended correction has been made and increase the opportunity for unwanted editing. [11] [12] [14]
The capsid that enables the vector to enter cells can also provoke immune responses that interfere with delivery. Antibodies acquired through earlier exposure to related viruses may neutralize the vector before it enters target cells, and antibodies generated by a first treatment can also make subsequent doses ineffective. Safety concerns can be serious for AAVs, and can include severe liver injury, with fatal acute liver failure reported following some systemic AAV treatments. [11] [12] [15] [17]
AAV therefore retains substantial drawbacks despite being among the most clinically established delivery platforms, creating intense need on the addressability problem for complex therapies.

Samsung's HBM revenue just passed SK hynix for the first time. At least, that's Bernstein's estimate: Q3 Samsung $8.7B vs SK hynix $7.6B.

Be clear on where that comes from. The report itself isn't public; I'm going off https://t.co/n6VSOfjT0S's and VLSI Korea's summaries. Bernstein back-calculated it from Korea's Jul–Sep HBM export data, and the Samsung figure actually came in ~10% below Bernstein's own earlier forecast.

On those numbers, Samsung grew +33% QoQ and SK hynix +11%. Both growing, Samsung much faster, on the HBM4 ramp. VLSI Korea cites Samsung's Q2 call: Q3 HBM4 revenue would be more than 3x the prior quarter.

But #1 in revenue isn't #1 at everything. Per reports cited by VLSI Korea, SK hynix is still the only one shipping 16-high HBM for Rubin in volume. The tallest stack is the hardest to build, and the easiest to sell.

Taiwan has a piece of this either way. SK hynix signed an MOU with TSMC (https://t.co/U2nKFTziDI / $TSM) in 2024: the HBM4 base die moves to TSMC logic process, and the HBM then goes into CoWoS alongside the GPU. Whoever sells the most HBM, the bottom of SK hynix's stack and the back-end packaging route through Taiwan.

So I'll wait for earnings: SK hynix Oct 28, Samsung Oct 29. If both disclose HBM revenue and HBM4 mix, we'll know whether Bernstein's number holds.

Not investment advice.

HBM4 16단 적층에서 두께 775마이크로미터가 사실상 전쟁의 승패를 가릅니다. TSMC CoWoS-L 위에 16단을 올리면 이 한계선에 부딪히는데, 플럭스리스 TC본더로 버틸 라인과 하이브리드 본딩으로 넘어갈 라인이 여기서 갈립니다.

핵심은 장비 서열입니다. SK하이닉스는 16단 초기 물량을 플럭스리스 TC본더로 소화하면서 하이브리드 본딩 전환 시점을 최대한 늦추는 쪽입니다. 기존 라인 자산을 살리면서 OPM 레버리지를 유지하는 판단입니다. 삼성전자는 하이브리드 본딩 조기 도입으로 수율 리스크를 정면 돌파하는 카드입니다. 마이크론은 장비 투자 여력이 상대적으로 얇아 검증된 TC본더 루트에 무게를 둡니다.

국내 밸류체인은 한미반도체의 TC본더 수주 잔고가 16단 전환 속도와 직결됩니다. 하이브리드 본딩은 장비 단가가 높아 초기 감가상각 부담이 OPM을 먼저 때립니다. 어느 라인이 먼저 16단 수율 60%를 넘기느냐가 관전 포인트입니다.

체크포인트는 하나입니다. 하이브리드 본딩 도입이 앞당겨질수록 2026년 HBM 설비투자에서 TC본더 발주가 꺾이는지 확인해야 합니다. 여러분은 16단에서 TC본더 연장과 하이브리드 본딩 조기 전환, 어느 쪽이 OPM에 유리하다고 보십니까.

"If you have only a certain amount of memory, you have to decide…"

Andy Jassy on the a16z podcast, Oct 23. I rewound this part twice.

First he lays out AWS capacity: '26 is sold out, '27 is largely sold out (with some held back for on-demand), and a good chunk of '28 is already gone. Then: data centers, power and memory are all finite, and he doesn't think the shortage ends in 2027.

Then the part I found most interesting. AI and what he calls the core (non-AI) business are both growing fast. Memory is fixed, so you decide how much goes to HBM for AI accelerators and how much to DRAM for the core business. His words: "real trade-offs."

He didn't say HBM is short, and he didn't name a single memory maker. He's talking from the buyer's side: the same pool of memory, and who gets it.

TrendForce said the same on Sep 29: AI server demand has HBM and conventional DRAM competing for the same advanced nodes and wafer capacity. On Sep 30 it forecast Q4 conventional DRAM contract prices up another 10–15%. Buyers are talking allocation; sellers are still raising prices.

Put that next to SemiAnalysis' view that HBM won't move to hybrid bonding until after 2029, and my read is: for the next three years HBM scales the way it's built today, while buyers are already rationing memory.

Taiwan angle, all my own inference (none of it is in the clip): ・Nanya (https://t.co/tFVc1fFjiK), Winbond (https://t.co/dNBGGQ8dic): if the big three tilt capacity to HBM, does conventional DRAM get tighter? ・TSMC (https://t.co/U2nKFTziDI) CoWoS: HBM ends up packaged next to GPUs and Trainium-class accelerators, so whatever slice goes to HBM moves the back end too?

What I haven't worked out: if even buyers are choosing between HBM and DRAM, who gets the remaining chunk of 2028 first? SK hynix reports Oct 28, Samsung Oct 29. I'll be listening for how they split capacity between HBM and conventional DRAM.

반도체 일주일 성적표가 나왔다. SOX -3.2%, 목요일 하루에만 -6.7%였다 📉

1. 장비주가 제일 크게 맞았다: 램리서치 -12.8%, 어플라이드 -7.8%, ASML -4.2%
2. 칩 설계·로직도 밀렸다: 인텔 -3.2%, AMD -2.3%, 브로드컴 -2.2%, 엔비디아 -1.5%
3. 그런데 메모리와 파운드리는 버텼다: 마이크론 -0.1%, SK하이닉스 +0.4%, 삼성전자 보합, TSMC +1.4%

공포의 정체는 AI 투자 청구서다. 
메타가 10년 만에 잉여현금흐름 마이너스(-21억 달러)를 냈고, 무의결권 주식 발행까지 꺼냈다. 그러자 빅테크가 장비 투자를 줄일 거라는 걱정이 장비주부터 때렸다.

하지만 수급 사이클은 아직 끝이 아니다 👇

1. 물량이 이미 묶여 있다. 증권가 추정으로 삼성은 2027년 메모리의 약 80%를 장기계약으로 잡았다. 마이크론도 2027년 물량의 75% 이상이 확정됐다고 했다.

2. 팹은 수도꼭지가 아니다. 클린룸 짓고 장비 들이고 수율 잡는 데 수년이 걸린다. 수요가 살아 있으면 공급은 바로 못 따라간다.

3. HBM은 더 까다롭다. 12단, 16단으로 쌓을수록 다이 하나만 불량이어도 스택 전체가 날아간다. 단수가 늘면 수율은 곱셈으로 깎인다.

4. 메모리를 다 만들어도 끝이 아니다. GPU 옆에 붙이는 첨단 패키징(CoWoS) 용량이 또 병목이다.

5. 이번 주 메모리주가 버틴 것도 시장이 이걸 알고 있는게 아닐까 생각된다.

반론도 있다. 빅테크가 내년 투자를 줄이면 장기계약도 재협상 테이블에 오른다. 그래서 지금은 "고점"보다 "증가율 정점" 논쟁에 가까워 보인다.
첫 시험대는 다음 주 SK하이닉스 실적(10/27)이다.

주가는 미래를 보기에 급등한 반도체의 숨고르기 시기일 뿐이다. 
피지컬 에이아이의 새로운 수급이 붙을 날이 머지않았다. 
2차 웨이브는 온다.

70–80 % de la surface de silicium d’un rack IA est de la mémoire. La HBM consomme 3 à 4 fois plus de wafers par Go que la DDR5.

Dylan Patel (SemiAnalysis) et Stacy Rasgon (Bernstein) viennent de partager leurs perspectives sur l'industrie des semi-conducteurs au CASPA CEO Summit.

Plusieurs déclarations importantes pour les investisseurs.

1️⃣ Les véritables goulots :

Dylan Patel classe les contraintes industrielles dans cet ordre :

1/Substrats avancés, PCB et matériaux.
2/Mémoire HBM et DRAM.
3/Lasers et composants optiques.
4/Équipements et capacités de fabrication.
5/Électricité et infrastructures.

Il estime que près de 50 GW de data centers seront en construction dans le monde en 2027.

Mais fabriquer suffisamment de substrats avancés pourrait être beaucoup plus difficile que trouver de nouvelles solutions d'alimentation électrique.

🇹🇼 Unimicron (3037), Kinsus (3189) et Nan Ya PCB (8046) sont particulièrement bien positionnés sur ce marché.

2️⃣ Le supercycle de la mémoire pourrait durer bien plus longtemps que prévu.

Stacy souligne un paradoxe :

Certains fabricants de mémoire se négocient entre 2 et 4 fois leurs bénéfices prévisionnels.

La HBM nécessite environ 3 à 4 fois plus de wafers que la DDR5 conventionnelle pour produire une quantité équivalente de mémoire.

Les nouvelles salles blanches ne permettront d'augmenter significativement les capacités qu'en 2028-2029.

Le marché anticipe déjà un effondrement des prix de la DRAM en 2028.

Sa question : « Et si cela ne se produisait pas ? »

🇰🇷 SK hynix, Samsung et 🇺🇸 Micron pourraient maintenir des bénéfices exceptionnellement élevés plus longtemps qu'anticipé.

3️⃣ NVIDIA commence à perdre des parts de marché face aux ASIC.

Selon Dylan, NVIDIA consomme déjà une proportion décroissante des capacités mondiales de HBM et de CoWoS.

Google, Amazon et AMD gagnent du terrain.

Mais attention : NVIDIA pourrait continuer à doubler ses bénéfices malgré cette baisse de part relative.

4️⃣ Le véritable enjeu sera la répartition des marges.

Dylan estime que le coût d'un GW d'infrastructure IA est passé d'environ 40 Md$ en 2024 à plus de 60 Md$ en 2026.

Une part considérable de cette valeur est captée par NVIDIA et les autres concepteurs de puces.

Si les hyperscalers internalisent davantage leur conception, une partie des profits pourrait se déplacer vers les fournisseurs de mémoire, de substrats et de composants industriels.

🇹🇼 Pour les investisseurs taïwanais, cela renforce l'intérêt de TSMC, Unimicron, Kinsus et Nan Ya PCB.

Le marché IA peut continuer à exploser sans que NVIDIA conserve indéfiniment la même part de la valeur.

📅 2027-2028 : pénuries 
2029 : première véritable interrogation sur le risque de surcapacités.  
CASPA CEO Summit, 23 octobre 2026.

今年以来算到10/23收盘， $ASX  涨了140.3%，$AMKR 跌了0.5%。

同样是封装测试龙头，同样站在AI链条上，一家翻了一倍多，一家原地没动。

这一篇讲产业链里的先进封装：$TSM 的CoWoS和SoIC，日月光（$ASX），$AMKR，再顺带设备和材料。

封装这一步做什么。

晶圆切出来的裸芯片，要装进封装、接上载板，才能焊到电路板上。

AI芯片难在密度：一颗GPU旁边要放好几叠HBM，彼此之间要拉成千上万条线，普通载板布不下。

CoWoS的办法，是在芯片和载板之间垫一块中介层，计算芯片和HBM并排放在上面，这叫2.5D。

台积电官网把它分成三种。

CoWoS-S用整块硅中介层，最大约3.3倍光罩尺寸。

CoWoS-R用聚合物加铜线做的RDL中介层。

CoWoS-L在RDL中介层里嵌入小块硅桥（LSI）负责芯片间的高密度连线，3.5倍光罩尺寸的版本2024年量产，超过3.3倍就要靠L或R。

SoIC换了个方向，把芯片直接上下叠起来，用铜对铜的混合键合连接，这叫3D。

CoPoS是把圆形晶圆换成方形面板来做中介层，一次能摆下更多大芯片。

谁是龙头，为什么。

CoWoS的龙头是台积电，10/15法说会上魏哲家的说法是，5倍光罩尺寸的CoWoS今天只有台积电在量产。

同一场会上，大摩分析师点名英特尔的EMIB-T，问客户选了对手、对手交付不了时，台积电愿不愿意接。

魏哲家先说尽量不直接回答，接着说：会。

产能还在追需求。TrendForce转引经济日报，台积电CoWoS月产能今年有望到12万至14万片，加上封测厂新增的5万至6万片，全行业接近20万片。

供需缺口从约20%收窄到年底约10%，TrendForce预计2.5D的严重短缺2027年开始缓和。

台积电做不完的部分，溢出给封测厂。

常见的分工是台积电做前段的芯片上晶圆（CoW），把组合好的模块交给封测厂接上载板（oS）、再做测试，部分厂也开始自己做整套2.5D。

日月光是全球最大的封测厂，TrendForce统计2024年前十大封测厂合计营收415.6亿美元，日月光185.4亿，接近45%；Amkor 63.2亿，排第二。

二季度日月光封测（ATM）营收1261.5亿新台币，同比增36%，毛利率27.3%。

上半年光是机器设备资本开支就花了27亿美元，厂房设施另有14亿。

封测收入里计算类的占比，从去年一季度的22%升到今年二季度的30%。

$AMKR 二季度毛利率16.8%，计算类占22%，和一年前一样；通讯类还占42%，前十大客户贡献66%的收入。

Amkor的牌是美国本土：亚利桑那园区投资扩大到约120亿美元，客户承诺已经超过一期3.3万平方米洁净室，二期计划2027年底开工、2029年底完工。

今年全年资本开支指引25亿至30亿美元，对一家季度营收不到20亿美元的公司，这是很重的投入。

10/9那条写过，$AMKR 和 $ASX 能不能从最高端AI封装拿到足够大的增量，要看实际订单。

二季度的毛利率和收入结构，日月光先交了答卷。

设备和材料各看一个点。

混合键合设备看Besi：三季度订单3.426亿欧元，同比增96.1%，今年的混合键合订单已经比2025全年翻了一倍还多，累计需求超过215台。

SemiAnalysis此前说ASML可能在开发同类设备，Besi的CEO这次回应，不把ASML看作混合键合的竞争者。

可四季度收入指引只是持平上下5%，公司说部分客户把交货对齐到2027年上半年的产能计划。

SoIC比CoWoS贵得多，TrendForce转引工商时报，每1万片月产能投资约68亿至70亿美元，台积电今年规划1万至1.5万片。

载板这一层卡在一块玻璃布上：ABF载板用的低膨胀T-glass，日东纺约占全球九成，福岛新产能2027年中才到市场，Tom's Hardware报道价格已经涨了20%至30%。

风险在供给追上来那一天。

10/9那条写的："当然，封装产能也不是永远稀缺。"

台积电在5月技术论坛给的数字是，2022到2027年CoWoS产能年复合增速超过80%。

路线也在变：CoPoS按TrendForce转引的时间表，2027年中试产，2028至2029年全面量产，面板一上来，设备和材料供应商要重新洗一遍。

EMIB-T如果做成，台积电的独家地位也要打折。

Yarı iletken sektöründe "yapay zeka ticareti" (AI trade) etrafındaki rallinin yerini belirli aralıklarla sert düzeltmelere ve konsolidasyona bırakması, sektörün temellerinin aniden çökmesinden ziyade **beklenti, değerleme ve sermaye harcaması (CapEx) dinamiklerinin yeniden fiyatlanmasından** kaynaklanıyor.

Bu soğumayı tetikleyen ana unsurlar şunlardır:

---

### 1. Yatırım Getirisi (ROI) ve Nakit Akışı Şüpheleri
Büyük bulut sağlayıcıları ve hiper ölçekleyiciler (Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, Amazon vb.) yapay zeka altyapısına yıllık yüz milyarlarca dolarlık sermaye harcaması (CapEx) yönlendiriyor. 
* **Gelir üretme gecikmesi:** Çip üreticileri (Nvidia, TSMC vb.) donanım satışlarıyla rekor kârlar elde ederken, bu altyapıyı satın alan yazılım ve internet devlerinin son kullanıcıdan elde ettiği doğrudan üretken yapay zeka gelirleri harcanan sermayenin hızına henüz tam anlamıyla yetişemedi.
* Piyasa şu soruyu sormaya başladı: *"Bulut devleri serbest nakit akışlarını bu hızda çip alımına yönlendirmeyi ne kadar sürdürebilir?"* Bu soru, harcama hızında olası bir duraklama ihtimalini fiyatlara yansıtıyor.

### 2. Aşırı Şişkin Değerlemeler ve Çarpan Sıkışması
2023–2024 ve 2025 boyunca sektör genelinde fiyat/kazanç (F/K) ve işletme değeri çarpanları tarihsel ortalamaların oldukça üzerine çıktı.
* Şirketler beklentileri aşan finansal sonuçlar (earnings beat) açıklasalar dahi, "kusursuzluk fiyatlanan" değerlemelerde en ufak bir büyüme yavaşlaması veya marj baskısı kâr realizasyonuna yol açıyor.
* Şirket kârları artmaya devam etse bile, piyasanın bu kârlara ödemeye razı olduğu katsayı (çarpan daralması) geriliyor.

### 3. Fiziksel Altyapı ve Enerji Darboğazları
Yarı iletken tedarik zincirinde talep güçlü kalsa da, veri merkezlerinin sahada ölçeklenmesi yeni fiziksel sınırlarla karşılaşıyor:
* **Elektrik şebekesi ve enerji kapasitesi:** Veri merkezlerinin ihtiyaç duyduğu gigawatt seviyesindeki elektrik gücünün şebekeye bağlanması, trafo ve türbin tedariki 12 ila 24 aya varan gecikmelere takılıyor.
* **Gelişmiş paketleme ve bellek (HBM):** TSMC'nin CoWoS kapasitesi ve yüksek bant genişlikli bellek (HBM3e/HBM4) arzı genişlemeye devam etse de, ısı dağıtımı ve soğutma altyapısı kurulumları teslimat sürelerini sınırlayarak çip dağıtım hızını yavaşlatıyor.

### 4. Makroekonomik Baskılar ve Sektörel Rotasyon
Yüksek faiz oranları ve tahvil getirileri, nakit akışlarının büyük bölümü uzak gelecekte gerçekleşecek yüksek çarpanlı büyüme hisselerini doğrudan iskonto ediyor. article.plain_text:
Estimate as of October 26, 2026. NVIDIA reports its next quarter (fiscal Q3 FY27, roughly August–October 2026) in mid-to-late November.
Bottom line
About 15 GW of new NVIDIA compute will be installed and actually powered on in 2027, with a reasonable range of 13–18 GW. That figure counts only the power drawn by the equipment in the racks (the "IT" basis). Including cooling and other facility overhead, the draw on the grid is about 18 GW.
The single most important assumption is how much NVIDIA earns per GW of Blackwell. Blackwell is NVIDIA's current GPU generation. I use $27B per GW. At the higher price management cited in 2025 ($30–35B), the answer falls to about 13.7 GW. If you take NVIDIA's February 2026 statement that roughly 9 GW of Blackwell was "deployed" and ignore the shipping-to-power-on lag (about $21B per GW), it rises to about 17.7 GW.
About a third of what powers on in 2027 is backlog, meaning GPUs sold in 2026 that do not get electricity until 2027. The other two-thirds come from shipments made in roughly January–September 2027. Going the other way, NVIDIA ships about 17 GW during 2027, but part of that will not be switched on until 2028.
Measured by work done, that is equivalent to about 23 GW of GB200 or 20 GW of GB300. GB200 and the upgraded GB300 are Blackwell's rack-scale products. Rubin, the next generation, began shipping in August 2026 and does roughly twice as much work per watt as Blackwell. So among the GPUs that power on in 2027, Blackwell accounts for about 58% of the power, while Rubin accounts for about 57% of the compute. (Both shares are medians of the model's simulations; dividing the central values directly gives numbers a point or two off.)
The whole industry adds about 22–27 GW (the model's 80% range). The widely quoted "43 GW of new AI compute in 2027" is SemiAnalysis's forecast of new data-center capacity worldwide across all vendors. It should be compared with the industry total, not with NVIDIA's 15 GW. On that comparison, SemiAnalysis's 43 GW is about 1.6–2 times the industry's 22–27 GW of chips. If you take investor Brad Gerstner's view that only about 25 GW can actually be built, the two are close to one-to-one. (Section 4.4 combines both views into a 1.0–2.1× range.)
The final formula. In plain terms: take what NVIDIA sells, divide by NVIDIA's revenue per GW, and subtract what has not yet been switched on.
GW powered on in 2027 (IT basis) = Σ over months of [NVIDIA data-center revenue × share that goes into GPU data centers × (Blackwell share ÷ Blackwell revenue per GW + Rubin share ÷ Rubin revenue per GW) × probability that a given month's shipments power on in 2027]
Conversions: grid-side GW = IT GW × PUE (total facility power ÷ IT power, about 1.2). GB200-equivalent GW = Blackwell GW × 1.1 + Rubin GW × 2.1. GB300-equivalent GW = GB200-equivalent ÷ 1.18. A hand calculation with central values is in 2.2; terms are defined in the Notes.
What each section answers:
 
 
1. Why NVIDIA's revenue can be turned into 2027 GW
In 2027 the bottleneck is likely to be chips, not data centers. NVIDIA supplies about two-thirds of new AI compute (measured by power), and it sells as much as it can get made. So revenue divided by revenue per GW gives the compute actually delivered.
1.1 The 2027 bottleneck is likely to be chips, so count chips
Data-center GW measure how much power a site is ready to accept; chip GW measure how much compute is actually plugged in. The two can diverge sharply by 2027. Data-center and grid construction is accelerating, while SemiAnalysis judged in October 2026 that chips could become the binding constraint, describing "memory and logic possibly becoming the new #1 constraint in 2027-28" (logic chips are the ones that do the computing, such as GPUs). When the constraint is on the chip side, compute should be counted from the seller of the chips.
1.2 NVIDIA supplies about two-thirds of new compute
Epoch AI tracks chip sales by power. By that measure, NVIDIA accounted for 65% of new AI compute in 2025 and 67% in the first half of 2026.
To scale from NVIDIA to the whole industry, I assume NVIDIA's share is 55%–68%. The lower end sits below Epoch's figure for two reasons:
Epoch records the power of Google's TPU v8i and Huawei's Ascend 950PR as zero, so it understates non-NVIDIA share and overstates NVIDIA's.
TPUs and AMD are both accelerating in 2027. Morgan Stanley estimates NVIDIA will account for only 45% of 2027 demand for CoWoS, TSMC's advanced packaging capacity (see 1.4).
1.3 NVIDIA's revenue is set by supply
Management's preliminary outlook is about 70% revenue growth in FY28, NVIDIA's fiscal year ending January 2028, which roughly matches calendar 2027. Management also said explicitly that supply sets this number. In the words of CEO Jensen Huang, according to the Motley Fool transcript: "even though our demand is much greater than 70%, our supply allows us to confidently deliver 70%." (Another transcript words it slightly differently.)
When demand exceeds supply, what gets sold is what gets made. So once you know how much NVIDIA earns per GW, dividing revenue by it gives the GW the supply chain actually delivers.
1.4 TSMC serves as a ceiling, not the main method
One view holds that a data-center GPU built without TSMC's leading-edge process and CoWoS packaging is not competitive on performance, so TSMC's CoWoS capacity is roughly the AI industry's compute capacity. (CoWoS packages the GPU together with high-bandwidth memory, or HBM.)
That view largely holds, for two reasons:
Google's TPU, Amazon's Trainium and AMD's GPUs all use TSMC process technology plus CoWoS.
Chips made outside TSMC are a small volume (see 4.2).
But converting CoWoS wafers into GW requires knowing how many good GPUs each wafer yields and whether there is enough HBM, and neither has reliable public data. So TSMC is used here for two things only: as a ceiling, since the GW implied by revenue should not exceed what CoWoS can support; and as a check on growth rates.
2. How money turns into GW, and what each parameter is
NVIDIA's revenue is split by month, divided by revenue per GW separately for each generation, and shifted into 2027 according to the power-on lag. Every parameter is a range, not a point.
2.1 The calculation chain
Take monthly NVIDIA data-center revenue and multiply by the share that goes into GPU data centers. This removes a small amount of revenue, such as RTX Pro servers and software, that does not end up in GPU data centers.
Split it by the revenue shares of Blackwell and Rubin, and divide each by its revenue per GW (how much NVIDIA revenue corresponds to one GW of compute). This gives GW shipped that month.
Shift shipments to the month they power on, using a distribution of shipping-to-power-on lags. This gives GW powered on that month.
Add up everything that lands in 2027 to get GW powered on in 2027 (IT basis).
Then convert: multiply by PUE for grid-side GW; multiply by performance-per-watt factors (2.7) for equivalent GW; divide by NVIDIA's share for the industry total.
The calculation is a Monte Carlo simulation: each run draws one value from each parameter's range and computes the result, 20,000 times in all. The "about 15 GW" in the text is the median of those 20,000 results; the "80% range" drops the top and bottom 10%.
2.2 A hand calculation with central values
The average lag from shipment to power-on is about four months, so "powered on in 2027" roughly equals "shipped between September 2026 and August 2027."
Remove revenue that does not go into GPU data centers. NVIDIA's data-center revenue over those 12 months is about $517B. Removing the 2.5% that does not go into GPU data centers leaves about $504B. Rubin is about 54% of it.
Divide by revenue per GW. Blackwell revenue of about $230B divided by $27B per GW is about 8.5 GW; Rubin revenue of about $274B divided by $40B per GW is about 6.8 GW. Together, about 15.3 GW.
Re-sort by actual power-on date. Four months is only an average: some systems power on earlier, some later, and a few wait for electricity. Working month by month, 15.2 GW lands in 2027, split by shipment batch into 8.8 GW of Blackwell and 6.4 GW of Rubin. Blackwell is higher and Rubin lower than in step 2 because most of what shipped in autumn 2026 was Blackwell, so most of what carries over into 2027 is Blackwell too. 15.2 GW × PUE of 1.2 gives about 18 GW on the grid side.
Convert to equivalent compute. 8.8 × 1.1 + 6.4 × 2.1 ≈ 23 GW GB200-equivalent; divided by GB300's factor of 1.18, about 19.5 GW GB300-equivalent. Here 1.1, 2.1 and 1.18 are the means of the parameter distributions; the table in 2.7 lists 1.10, 1.9 and 1.15, which are the modes (most likely values). That is why the two sets of numbers differ.
A rougher shortcut skips the monthly split: FY28 shipments ≈ FY28 data-center revenue × 97.5% × (Blackwell share ÷ $27B + Rubin share ÷ $40B). This gives shipments for FY28 (February 2027–January 2028), about 0.6 GW more than calendar-2027 shipments. It also counts shipments, not power-on; for that, see 3.3.
2.3 Revenue
Confidence in the tables below comes in three grades: "high" means company filings or primary data; "medium" means secondary reports, management's spoken remarks, or several sources that agree; "low" means judgment calls, single sources, or search snippets only.
 
The FY27 Q3 mode sits slightly above guidance because NVIDIA has generally beaten its guidance by a small margin in recent years. The FY28 range extends down to 50% to cover a demand slowdown.
2.4 Revenue per GW is priced on IT load
The firmest evidence is in NVIDIA's 10-Q (its quarterly filing), which describes the PORTS-Pike campus as "approximately 4.25 gigawatts of IT load." Kress's written commentary says each generation of infrastructure there "could represent" about 1.5 million GPUs and $150–200B of revenue. Spread over 4.25 GW, that is about $35–47B per GW, consistent with Rubin's $40B. So this estimate reads revenue per GW as an IT-basis figure. Confidence: medium.
The earnings calls never define which GW they mean. If revenue per GW is actually priced on grid-side power, the same revenue buys fewer IT GW, because revenue per IT GW must be multiplied by PUE. Applying that to Rubin alone lowers 2027 to 14.1 GW; applying it to both Blackwell and Rubin lowers it to 12.7 GW. This is one source of the lower end of the reasonable range (see 4.6).
2.5 What NVIDIA earns per GW: the parameter that matters most
According to third-party transcripts such as Motley Fool's (NVIDIA's official PDF was not available), Jensen Huang gave revenue per GW for three generations on the August 2026 earnings call: "In the case of Hopper, we were at about $18 billion per gigawatt. For Grace Blackwell, we're about $25 billion per gigawatt. And for Vera Rubin, it's about $40 billion per gigawatt."
The Blackwell figure does not match what he said earlier. In November 2025 he put Grace Blackwell at "$30 billion plus or minus," and in August 2025 he said NVIDIA's share of a one-GW data center was about $35B. So Blackwell needs independent evidence. The table below tests it against three anchors:
 
How each anchor is computed:
The first anchor: Epoch counts about 2.33 million B300 and 0.57 million B200 shipped by NVIDIA in the first half of 2026. Taking each GPU's IT power as rack power ÷ 72 gives about 5.5 GW in total; data-center revenue over the same period was about $155B, which gives $28.3B per GW.
The second anchor: Epoch puts NVIDIA's 2025 chip TDP at about 4.9 GW. Multiplying TDP by 1.4–1.5 to get IT power gives about 6.8–7.3 GW; FY26 data-center revenue of $193.7B then gives $26–28B per GW.
Neither of these is independent: Epoch derives NVIDIA's unit counts from NVIDIA's revenue divided by unit prices, so they only show consistency with Epoch's price assumptions.
The third anchor: if "deployed" means powered on, then with a four-month lag those 9 GW can only correspond to about $127B of shipments made before October 2025; with no lag and counting through January 2026, about $188B. The resulting $14–21B is clearly low. The 9 GW may include systems shipped but not yet powered on, may be on a grid-side basis, or may simply be a round number.
Values used in the model:
Blackwell: $22–32B, mode $27B. Confidence medium. This is a gross figure: total data-center revenue is the numerator. Management's earlier $30–35B is not used because both Epoch anchors fall at $26–28B. Instead, the earlier figure drives the low-GW scenario and the strict reading of "9 GW" drives the high-GW scenario (see 4.6).
Share that goes into GPU data centers: deduct only 0–5%. Confidence low. When Kress discussed Rubin, she said revenue per GW already includes the Vera CPU, LPU (NVIDIA's inference accelerator) and networking.
Rubin: $34–46B, mode $40B. Confidence medium. PORTS-Pike implies $35–47B; the model uses a symmetric range centered on $40B. There is no Rubin shipment data yet to test it.
2.6 Generation mix, shipping-to-power-on lag, and facility overhead
 
Rubin share: the Q3 figure of 20% is from Kress: "We see Vera Rubin accounting for about 20% of data center revenue in Q3." Later quarters draw on two pieces of information: on the Q1 FY27 call, management said the first quarter of FY28 would be "very big"; TrendForce says GB300 will carry through the first half of 2027 and that VR200 (Rubin's rack-scale product) will be the highest-volume product of 2027.
Shipping-to-power-on lag: ODMs (contract manufacturers) take about 1–2 months to assemble a rack, then shipping, installation and commissioning take another 1–3 months. CoreWeave added more than 300 MW of active power in the single month of June 2026.
PUE does not go as low as 1.1 at the bottom of the range. SemiAnalysis's InferenceX benchmark implies about 1.1 and Google's fleet averages 1.09, but both come from best-in-class operators. New liquid-cooled AI data centers generally target below 1.3, and the industry average will be above the best operators.
2.7 Performance per watt, used for equivalent GW
Relative to GB200, on an IT-power basis. FP8 and FP4 are two numerical precisions; lower precision computes faster. "Dense" means rated compute without sparsity speedups.
 
Blackwell: on specifications, dense FP8 compute is unchanged while power is about 15% higher, so about 0.86× for training; FP4 inference is about 1.29×. InferenceX throughput per MW measured 0.93–1.13× for DeepSeek R1 and 1.36–4.1× for V4 Pro.
Rubin can be estimated from specifications in two ways. Token generation is limited by memory bandwidth: 19.2–22 TB/s per GPU ÷ 2.64–3.19 kW gives about 1.26–1.74× GB200. Dense compute ÷ power gives about 1.8–2.2×. NVIDIA's marketing claim that Vera Rubin "delivers up to 10x more tokens per megawatt than NVIDIA GB200 NVL72" picks the most favorable operating point and is not used.
The GB300 factor and the blended Blackwell factor are drawn independently in the model, so the GB300-equivalent range is slightly wider than it would otherwise be.
3. The numbers
About 15 GW powers on in 2027, equivalent to about 23 GW of GB200. About 5 GW of it is backlog from 2026.
3.1 Physical GW: about 15 GW powers on in 2027
"Powered on" below means the data center is energized and the GPUs start working.
 
Figures in parentheses are 80% ranges.
On a calendar-year basis, NVIDIA's data-center revenue rises from about $362B in 2026 to about $620B in 2027, up about 71%, but shipments rise only from 12.5 GW to 17.2 GW, up about 38%. The difference is the rise in revenue per GW: blending Blackwell and Rubin, it goes from about $28.3B to about $34.8B, up about 23%. Roughly, six-tenths of NVIDIA's revenue growth comes from selling more GW and four-tenths from charging more per GW.
3.2 Measured by work done: about 23 GW of GB200, 20 GW of GB300
 
The equivalent-GW range is much wider than the physical one, and most of the uncertainty is Rubin's performance per watt. There are no public Rubin measurements yet: the InferenceX comparison page is empty, and MLPerf (the industry-standard benchmark) 6.0 has no Rubin results. This is the softest link in the whole estimate.
Converting to H100-equivalent GW depends on the workload. On specifications for training, GB200's performance per watt is about 1.9× H100's; measured inference on large MoE (mixture-of-experts) models is 8–23×. So "how many H100-equivalent GW come online in 2027" could be anything from 45 GW to over 200 GW. That number carries too little information to be useful here.
3.3 About a third of what powers on in 2027 is 2026 backlog
 
What flows into 2027 and what flows out of it are different generations. The roughly 5.2 GW shipped in 2026 and powered on in 2027 is mostly GB300; the roughly 7.3 GW shipped in 2027 and powered on in 2028 is mostly Rubin. That is why, counted by power-on, 2027 is still a Blackwell year.
Because shipments grow every quarter, more flows out of 2027 than flows in, so 2027's power-on total is about 2 GW below its shipments (15.2 GW versus 17.2 GW).
The naive one-step division gives 15.5–25.6 GW, too wide to use. The Appendix explains why it was dropped and how the model evolved.
4. Does the result hold up?
Evidence points both ways: slightly more items suggest the true figure could be higher than the model, while three suggest it could be lower. The reasonable range is 13–18 GW.
4.1 Summary
The "Direction" column gives the direction of the true value relative to the model: ↑ means the true figure may be higher than the model, ↓ means it may be lower, ≈ means agreement. The tables in 4.3 and 4.5 use the same notation.
 
4.2 How much TSMC packaging and high-bandwidth memory can support
Tests: the ceiling on 2027 shipments. Independent? Partly. The CoWoS wafer counts come from independent sources, but converting wafers to GW uses the same Rubin share and per-GPU power assumptions as the model.
Capacity trajectory: TSMC's monthly CoWoS capacity was about 65–75k wafers at end-2025 (Epoch), will be about 120–140k at end-2026, and about 170–200k at end-2027. The end-2027 figure has two sources: KGI said 170k in March 2026, noting that "expansion will mainly happen in 2H27F"; Morgan Stanley says 200k but does not say whether that is a year-end or full-year monthly average. That implies about 1.8–2.0M wafers for full-year 2027.
NVIDIA used about 377k wafers in 2025, or 59% (Epoch). Morgan Stanley estimates NVIDIA's 2027 demand at 1.222M wafers, or 45%. That 45% is a share of Morgan Stanley's estimate of global demand (2.694M wafers), and the demand figure itself exceeds the TSMC supply estimated above, so it is not on the same basis as the 1.8–2.0M. Another estimate, counting only CoWoS-L (one CoWoS variant), is about 910k wafers; it also comes from Morgan Stanley and was seen only in a search snippet.
Converting to GW (my estimate): good GPUs per wafer are taken as 8.5–10 for B300 (the chip in GB300), based on about 9 back-calculated from Epoch's data, and 7–9 for Rubin, based only on an old JPMorgan estimate of 9. Rubin is 60%–70% of NVIDIA's wafers.
 
The low scenario averages about 6.8 GPUs per wafer, below both ranges above, because the three scenarios assume 90%, 95% and 100% of wafers, respectively, go to GPUs; the rest go to switch chips and other parts.
Verdict: no constraint in the mid and high scenarios; a binding one in the low scenario. Revenue implies 17.2 GW of 2027 shipments.
The low scenario's ceiling is only 14 GW, below the model's 17.2 GW. HBM may also bind before CoWoS does. Four signs point that way:
In September 2026 TrendForce said: "TrendForce expects the HBM market to remain supply-constrained in 2027."
HBM bit shipments are expected to grow 50%–60% in 2027, slower than the 70%–90% growth in CoWoS wafers.
KGI said Rubin's share of CoWoS in 2026 was pushed below half because HBM4 supply fell short.
NVIDIA's supply commitments rose from $119B to $279B in Q2 FY27, with the increase mainly for memory purchases, another sign that memory is the constraint.
All of these point to downside risk.
The mid scenario's wafers could support more than 20 GW, above the 17.2 GW implied by revenue. There are two possible explanations: either NVIDIA earns less per GW than assumed, so actual shipments exceed the model; or some chips packaged in 2027 do not ship until 2028.
"Chips not made at TSMC are not competitive" largely holds. The largest non-TSMC AI chip is Huawei's Ascend, at about 800k units in 2025 (SemiAnalysis); CFR estimates its 2026 compute at about 4% of NVIDIA's. Intel's EMIB-T packaging will reach about 15–20k wafers per month by 2027 (in CoWoS-equivalent terms). By my rough estimate, non-TSMC AI chips amount to less than 5%–10% of NVIDIA's power, so "TSMC advanced-packaging capacity ≈ industry compute capacity" is a reasonable approximation. Note, though, that TPU, Trainium and AMD are also inside TSMC's capacity and take about half of CoWoS.
4.3 Rack and unit counts from the supply chain and analysts
Tests: shipped GW. Independent? Yes; none of these numbers were used to set parameters. But converting rack counts to GW uses one shared set of rack-power assumptions (190–230 kW per rack, from Ming-Chi Kuo and server maker 2CRSi).
 
Three of these need a word more:
Wolfe: its 2026 Rubin rack count disagrees with both Kuo and Kress, and Wolfe is the one that is high. For 2027, Rubin alone matches the model; adding Rubin Ultra suggests actual shipments could exceed it.
Morgan Stanley's 7-million figure: 90k racks × 72 ≈ 6.5 million, so the 7 million looks like a package count. But if it really is packages, Rubin revenue would have to reach about $800B, more than NVIDIA's entire data-center revenue.
TrendForce: $710B of rack value already exceeds NVIDIA's data-center revenue, because it includes non-NVIDIA content such as assembly and memory; neither the rack count nor the unit price is transparent.
4.4 Third-party statistics: more data centers than chips
Tests: the relationship between data centers and chips. These sources count data-center capacity, so they cannot show whether chip counts are too high or too low.
 
4.5 What buyers and NVIDIA itself say
Tests: power-on volume. Independent? See each row.
 
The neocloud row points ↑ because neoclouds' net additions in 2026 alone equal half of the model's 2026 NVIDIA power-on (9.9 GW).
4.6 Where the 13–18 GW reasonable range comes from
The 80% range (14.1–16.5) reflects only parameter uncertainty. The reasonable range also accounts for definitional ambiguity and data conflicts:
Low end, about 13 GW. Three cases land here:
Blackwell revenue per GW at about $32B, per management's 2025 remarks: rerunning gives 13.7 GW.
Revenue per GW priced on grid-side power: 14.1 GW if applied to Rubin only, 12.7 GW if applied to both Blackwell and Rubin.
The CoWoS low scenario capping shipments (14 GW), which corresponds to about 13 GW powered on.
High end, about 18 GW. Two cases land here:
Blackwell revenue per GW at about $21B, from reading the ~9 GW "deployed" remark with no lag: rerunning gives 17.7 GW.
TrendForce's rack counts: at least 20 GW shipped, which at the same shipment-to-power-on ratio is about 18 GW powered on.
5. Which parameters matter most
Physical GW depends mostly on what NVIDIA earns per GW; equivalent GW depends mostly on how fast Rubin really is.
5.1 Rank correlation: which parameter matters most
The rank correlation coefficient measures how strongly the result moves when a parameter rises. The larger the absolute value, the bigger the effect; a negative sign means a larger parameter gives a smaller result.
 
FY28 growth matters little because most of the extra shipments in the second half of 2027 do not power on until 2028.
The table below is a quick lookup of FY28 shipments (GW, IT basis) for different values of FY28 data-center revenue and Rubin's revenue share. It uses the shortcut formula in 2.2 with point values on an FY28 basis, so it runs about 0.6–1 GW above the model's calendar-2027 shipments (17.2 GW).
 
Each 10-percentage-point rise in Rubin's share cuts about 0.7–0.9 GW; each additional $45B of revenue adds about 1.1–1.5 GW (computed cell by cell from the table).
5.2 If Rubin slips: physical GW barely changes, compute falls 2%–7%
Suppose HBM4 or yield problems cut Rubin's share by 15 percentage points across the board from FY27 Q4, with GB300 filling the gap. There are two cases: total revenue unchanged, which requires spare GB300 capacity; or FY28 revenue 10% lower.
 
Physical GW barely changes because Blackwell is cheaper per GW, so the same money buys more watts. Of the two cases, lower revenue is the more realistic: memory is already a constraint (see 4.2), so GB300 may not have spare capacity to fill in.
5.3 If some backlog lasts over a year: at most about 1 GW more
The model assumes most shipments power on within 2–6 months, with only 0–15% waiting a further 6 months, so 2025 shipments contribute nothing to 2027. If in reality some GPUs sit for more than a year, the model misses them. (Satya Nadella has said Microsoft had chips it could not plug in; I saw this remark only in a search snippet.) About 9 GW shipped from the second half of 2025 through the first half of 2026. Every 5% of that slipping into 2027 adds about 0.45 GW to 2027; even a 10% slip adds only about 1 GW.
6. Are some common intuitions right?
The common intuitions are broadly right. Two need correcting: NVIDIA's share should be revised down, and Rubin is not stuck in a queue. It has already shipped and is waiting for power.
"NVIDIA has 70%–80% of the market, so the others can be ignored." Slightly too high. Epoch puts it at 65%–67%, and since Epoch understates other vendors, NVIDIA's true share is lower still. TPUs and AMD are both accelerating in 2027: sell-side forecasts have TPU shipments rising from 3.2–4.5 million to 5.0–7.9 million units (seen only in search snippets), and AMD has won a first 1 GW each from OpenAI and Anthropic. TPU and Trainium use the same advanced TSMC capacity and cannot be ignored. The industry figure is NVIDIA's divided by 0.55–0.68. The direction is right, though: work out NVIDIA and you have worked out about two-thirds.
"GB200/GB300 cost two to three times as much as H100. Are they four to five times as capable?" Four to five times is a reasonable estimate for a mixed workload, but the comparison has to be per GW, not per GPU. Revenue per GW went from $18B for Hopper to $25B for Grace Blackwell (Jensen Huang's figures on the earnings call, see 2.5), only about 1.4 times. Performance per watt, meanwhile, is about 1.9× for training (specification) and 8–23× for large-model inference (measured). So each dollar buys more compute. The claim that "H100 can't run frontier models" is, strictly, that it can't run them economically: frontier MoE models with long context need a 72-GPU interconnect domain like NVL72. H100 has only 8-GPU nodes, and that is where the 8–23× gap in throughput per MW comes from.
"New capacity in 2027 is mostly GB200/GB300; Rubin is still in the queue." Counted by physical GW powered on, this is right: Blackwell is 58%. But counted by shipments, Rubin is already about 61%, and by effective compute about 57%. So Rubin is not in a queue. It has already shipped and is waiting for power.
"What powers on in 2027 should include GPUs sold earlier but not yet powered on." Correct, and that is how the model works. About a third comes from 2026 backlog (see 3.3).
7. Limitations, and what to watch after the next earnings report
Limitations
Rubin has no measured data. Its revenue per GW and its performance per watt are both estimates, the main reason the equivalent-GW range is wide.
The three anchors for Blackwell revenue per GW disagree, and two of them rely on Epoch's price assumptions. Yet this is the parameter with the biggest effect on physical GW (see 5.1).
The 80% range reflects only parameter uncertainty. Uncertainty from definitions and data conflicts is captured in the reasonable range in 4.6.
China is excluded. China is not in NVIDIA's guidance; if exports are allowed, that is additional volume.
Revenue is assumed to be set entirely by supply. If demand weakens, revenue will fall short. This estimate covers only "how much can be delivered," not "whether buyers can absorb it."
The 2026 power-on figure has no independent check. No power-on data exist to test the 9.9 GW.
After the next earnings report (FY27 Q3, mid-to-late November), update:
Data-center revenue and Rubin's share: is Q3 about 20%, and how high does Q4 climb?
The revenue per GW management cites, especially whether Rubin goes above $40B.
Supply-chain rack counts, and whether Morgan Stanley's 7-million figure counts packages or dies. This is the unresolved conflict with the largest effect.
Quarterly growth in active power (electricity actually in use) at neoclouds such as CoreWeave and Nebius. This is the number closest to "actually powered on."
 
Notes: definitions
GW, IT basis, grid-side basis. A GW (gigawatt) is one million kilowatts. The IT basis counts only electricity used by GPUs, CPUs and networking equipment in the racks. The grid-side basis is the total electricity a data center draws from the grid, including cooling and power-distribution losses. The ratio of the two is PUE, about 1.2 for new liquid-cooled AI data centers. NVIDIA prices revenue per GW on IT load (2.4), so revenue translates directly into IT GW. Use the grid-side basis when asking how much extra power the grid and generators must supply.
Fiscal year. NVIDIA's fiscal year ends in late January: FY27 roughly equals calendar 2026, and FY28 roughly equals calendar 2027. The model works month by month, which handles the one-month offset.
Shipment and power-on. Shipment is when NVIDIA recognizes revenue; power-on is when the data center is energized and the GPUs start working. The two are about four months apart on average.
Equivalent GW. How many GW of GB200 (or GB300) racks it would take to match a batch of GPUs' compute, used to compare the working capacity of different generations.
Median, mode. The median is the middle value of the 20,000 simulation results. The mode is the most likely value within a parameter's range.
Other abbreviations.
 
Appendix: how the model evolved
All figures in the text come from the final version (v3). The table records earlier versions and the problems found in each.

"병목에서 해자로"

AI의 진짜 해자는 진입 장벽에서 나온다. 부족함(병목)은 시간이 지나면 풀리지만 진입 장벽은 남는다. 그래서 AI 인프라는 병목이 아니라 해자로 봐야 한다.

미국 장기채 금리는 크게 올랐지만 회사채 스프레드는 안정적이다. 금리 상승을 이끈 것은 신용 위험이 아니라 텀 프리미엄이다. 위험은 채권 시장에만 머물러 있고, 주식에 주는 충격은 아직 제한적이다.

한국 투자자 예탁금은 6월 고점 이후 줄었고, 미국 개인 순매수도 평균을 밑돈다. 아직 들어오지 않은 대기 자금이 많다는 뜻이며, 모두가 들어온 상태가 아니므로 고점 신호로 보기 어렵다.

기관은 올해 개별 주식을 팔고 인덱스와 ETF를 샀다. 개별 주식 포지션이 가볍고, 기술주는 7월 이후 되사는 중이다. 이벤트 불확실성이 걷히면 관심은 10월 실적과 AI 모델로 옮겨갈 것이다.

자동차, PC 산업처럼 AI도 생산은 늘고 기업 수는 줄어드는 성숙 단계에 들어섰다. 프런티어 AI 기업은 마진은 높지만 R&D 경쟁 때문에 적자다. 스마일 커브상 해자는 양 끝(반도체 인프라, 거대 플랫폼)에 있고, 진입 장벽은 자본 집약도, 기술적 복합성, 축적된 노하우, 제도적 보호의 네 가지로 나뉜다.

미국 중간 선거에서 민주당이 우세해지면 데이터센터 투자에 제동이 걸릴 수 있고, 시장이 이를 선반영하는 것으로 본다. 악재가 모두 반영된 수준은 코스피 6천대 초반이며, 과거 공포 국면 데이터상 이 구간 매수는 대체로 1~3개월 안에 수익이 났다.

파운드리와 선단 공정(자본 집약도, TSMC 실적), 메모리와 HBM(노하우와 수율, SK하이닉스 실적), 전력 기기와 변압기(숙련 인력, 버티브 실적), 건설·전력·원전(제도, 선별 접근)으로 구성한다.

원칙: 종목은 해자로, 비중은 규칙으로
AI 사이클은 긴 호흡으로 보고 변동성은 베타 규칙으로 관리한다. 국내는 에너지, 산업재, IT가 매력적이고 밸류 트랩은 거른다. 해외도 에너지(낮은 PER)와 IT(72주 연속 이익 상향) 비중 확대.

금리가 안정돼야 멀티플이 확장되며, 이익이 뒷받침되는 저평가 섹터가 수혜를 본다. 기저 효과로 2027년 상반기 CPI가 둔화(5월 1.91% 추정)될 수 있고, 11월 QRA에서 재무부가 장기물 공급을 줄이면 텀 프리미엄이 꺾일 수 있다. 이때 한국 같은 저평가 국가로 자금이 이동할 가능성이 높다.

VIX 35 근처와 변동성 확대 시 미국 비중 축소, 코스피가 20일선(6,900~7,000)을 회복 못 하면 한국 비중 축소, CPI에서 유가가 물가로 번지면 주식 축소하되 에너지 유지, 유가 급락 시 에너지 축소 검토. 가장 좋은 경우는 10년 금리 하락 전환으로, 밸류에이션 리레이팅과 숏 포지션 청산까지 나올 수 있다.

OCP 글로벌 서밋(12~15일), 미국 CPI와 ASML(14일), 엔비디아 GTC(20일), TSMC와 IBM(21일), 테슬라·램리서치·인텔·버티브(같은 주), SK하이닉스(28일 전후). 악재가 이미 반영된 수준이라면 바이 더 딥이 유효하다.

한국은 현금 15%를 선택권으로 두고 추세 회복 시 AI 인프라 중심으로 채운다. 미국은 기준 비중 100% 유지하되 늘리지 않고 빅테크와 소프트웨어로 분산한다. 얼마를 담을지는 규칙으로, 무엇을 담을지는 해자로 고른다.

THE AI DIP: THE MARKET REPRICED THE BILL, NOT THE BUILD

October took the AI complex apart. Meta grew revenue 26% and got sold. Lam Research printed record revenue and fell 12% in a day. $TSMC guided to 58% growth and the selloff did not even pause. When the strongest demand prints of the year land and prices still fall, the problem is not demand. The problem is what the market will pay for the build — and what it now charges to fund it.

My read: roughly 80% of this dip is multiple compression and a credit repricing. About 20% is real — and that 20% lives in the financing layer, where CoreWeave's credit trades above 1,000bp and Oracle sits one notch above junk against $288B of off-balance-sheet leases.

THE STACK, LAYER BY LAYER

1. Compute silicon — $NVDA, $AVGO, $AMD. Demand is supply-limited, not demand-limited. Nvidia guides $108B for the quarter; Broadcom carries a $73B AI backlog. Bottleneck: CoWoS packaging and HBM, not wafers.

2. Networking and optical — $COHR, $LITE, $ANET. The fastest-growing layer in the stack: 800G+ transceiver shipments go from ~24M units to ~63M in one year. Also the most dislocated: Coherent is down 53% from its high on an intact 1.6T ramp, with Nvidia itself investing $2B each into Coherent and Lumentum to secure supply.

3. Memory — $MU, SK Hynix, Samsung. The tightest physical market in the stack. HBM is sold out, DRAM contract prices rose 90%+ in a single quarter, and inventories are under ten days. Micron fell 22% in a month inside a shortage. That is a pullback, not a broken thesis.

4. Power and cooling — $VRT, $ETN, $GEV. Half of the US capacity planned for 2026 is delayed or cancelled. Transformer lead times are 128-144 weeks. The bottleneck is not generation — it is energisation. Vertiv reports Oct 28 with a $15B backlog; that print tells us if power orders slow with sentiment.

5. Buildout and neoclouds — $CRWV, $ORCL, $NBIS. Growth is real CoreWeave revenue +112%, backlog $104B and so is the leverage. This layer does not bottom on the equity bouncing — it bottoms when the credit does: CDS back under 1,000bp, bonds back above 80-85 cents, a clean refinancing.

6. Cloud, models and apps — $MSFT, $GOOGL, $AMZN. Roughly $713-733B of 2026 capex across the big four, against Google Cloud +82%, Azure +40%+, and contracted backlogs in the hundreds of billions. Oct 28-29 is the monetisation verdict.

7. Security — $CRWD, $PANW, $FTNT. More AI means more attack surface, and this layer outperformed during the selloff. The risk here is not demand, it is valuation — near 50x sales, there is no dip to buy. It is a hold, not an add.

THE NEXT BOTTLENECK

After compute: financing binds first (H1 2027 — 15-19 year leases against 5-year contracts and 3-5 year GPU lives), power binds everywhere (a 2,061GW interconnection queue, 61-month median wait), memory binds through 2027, and co-packaged optics binds 2028-29 if it slips.

WHY THE LONG TERM HAS NOT CHANGED

Demand is contracted, not hoped: Microsoft RPO $627-678B, Google Cloud backlog ~$514B, AWS backlog rising through $364-496B, Oracle $664B. Cloud growth is accelerating while capex rises — capacity is the constraint, not demand. Every next generation of silicon raises power, bandwidth and memory intensity per rack. October repriced the multiple on that path. It did not produce one major guide-down of the path itself.

the next two weeks are verdict weeks: Fed Oct 28, Alphabet and Microsoft Oct 28, Amazon Oct 29, Nvidia Nov 17-18. So we scale in on tranches where the levels hold, size the levered names smaller, keep dry powder for the prints — and we do not average down into a name whose credit, not just its chart, has broken.

This is not the time to quit the AI trade. It is the time to own the shortage layers at October prices, and let the financing layers prove themselves first.

This week's research tested quantum computing from the outside. An outside team ran error correction on a rented $IBM chip. A proof showed photon loss lets a normal computer imitate one photonic advantage test, a question for $XNDU and its peers. And IBM linked two processors with 80 centimeters of cable.
My question: does each result hold when someone else checks it? I curated 52 papers from arXiv's October 19 to 23 listings. A reading sample, not a census.
 
1. Error correction you can rent
Below-threshold error correction used to come from the hardware's builders. This week, researchers from Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, Fordham, the University of Washington and NASA Ames did it on a cloud IBM processor, with no IBM authors.
Below threshold means the trade works: spend more physical qubits on one logical qubit, and its error rate falls. Growing a surface code from distance 3 to 6, the logical error per round fell from about 0.5% to about 0.2%, a suppression factor of 1.68 and 1.85 in the two bases. In runs of up to 150 rounds the advantage weakened. (Paper)
For scale, Quantinuum's ($QNT) color code reports a factor of about 12 on Helios. Different code, different machine, run by the vendor and decoded after the run, so it is no like-for-like race. (Paper)
That one number sets how many physical qubits each logical qubit will cost. For investors, a result an outsider can reproduce on rented hardware is worth more than a vendor's slide. I now ask: which suppression factor, over how many rounds, and with which decoder?
 
2. Reality checks on quantum advantage
BosonSampling sends photons through a maze of beam splitters and records where they land. Copying those patterns on a normal computer is believed to be extremely hard, which made it a leading test for quantum advantage.
But real devices lose photons, and loss makes the patterns easier to imitate. Go and Jeong at Seoul National University show a classical computer keeps up whenever any fixed share survives, even a large one. (Paper)
The limit matters. The proof covers standard BosonSampling. Xanadu's 2022 advantage experiment, like the other largest ones, used a Gaussian variant, so this does not settle those claims.
Classical methods pushed elsewhere too. A classical algorithm grew the distinct solutions from QuEra's Aquila on 43 graph problems by a median 24.3x, sometimes beating the hardware. (Paper) A randomized classical simulation method matched standard deterministic calculations with several orders of magnitude less memory. (Paper)
For investors, an advantage claim is only as strong as the best classical attempt to match it. For photonics, ask how many photons survive, and whether that share rises as the machine grows.
 
3. Linking machines, from a meter to a city
Most roadmaps reach large machines by connecting smaller ones.
IBM joined two 120-qubit Nighthawk processors with 80 centimeters of superconducting cable. Moving a state across worked at 99.00% mean fidelity, but a two-qubit gate between the processors averaged 94.75%, because one cross-cable gate is built from several steps whose errors add up. (Paper)
At city scale, a University of Innsbruck team ran a trapped-ion repeater node over 17 km of deployed fiber, at 81.6% fidelity. (Paper)
For any modular roadmap, IBM's included, the gate between modules, not the cable, decides whether modules add up to one computer.
 
Also this week
KTH · Decoders. A consumer NVIDIA ($NVDA) RTX 5080 reached 91% of a data-center GPU's decoding throughput, on simulated data. (Paper)
JPMorganChase and Quantinuum · Logic. They report at least a tenfold spacetime cut over the surface code for the magic states behind universal logic. (Paper)
Quantum Motion · Silicon spins. Proposed a high-rate code that assumes shuttling about ten times better than today. (Paper)
Results get stronger when someone else can check them.

Five Qubits. All Running. 99.9% Accurate.

RIKEN researchers report running five silicon spin qubits at the same time while keeping about 99.9% accuracy across all five.

They traced a major source of error to the microwave control signals, then corrected it with a calibration between pairs of qubits instead of calibrating every combination. A single qubit alone reached well above 99.99%, and up to three running together stayed above 99.99%. The study is in Nature Physics, and the release was posted October 25.

The caveats matter. These are single-qubit gates on five qubits. No two-qubit results were reported, and the remaining errors come from the higher microwave power needed to run several qubits at once. It is a step toward fault tolerance, not a threat to any cryptography today.

Why it matters here: this is a third kind of hardware progress in under two weeks, after trapped-ion error correction and Google's error-reduction work. Different qubit technologies keep improving.

QuanChain does not bet on one of them. Its oracle tracks the cost per logical qubit-hour & wallets move to stronger security levels at their next spend.

The progress comes from every direction. The design should not depend on which one wins.

On quantum stock Infleqition $INFQ: 

The crown jewel of Infleqtion’s sensing business: a compact atomic clock called Tiqker, which keeps precise time for up to a week without GPS.

Q2 revenue was $13.5 million, up 157% from the year before. First half 2026 revenue was $23.4 million. Fully-year 2026 revenue guidance is about $45.1 million.

Infleqtion’s growth has come entirely from its own quantum business, not acquisitions. The biggest recent growth driver is its quantum gravity sensor program with NASA. In August, NASA added a $20 million follow-on contract for that program. And earlier this month, the UK awarded Infleqtion £9 million to build a quantum radio-frequency sensing system with defense contractor Leonardo.

The computing side is also gaining traction. Infleqtion delivered the UK’s first and only operational 100-qubit quantum computer to its National Quantum Computing Centre, and it delivered a system in Japan.

Meanwhile, the company has an inked contract to install a quantum computer at the Illinois Quantum & Microelectronics Park in 2027. This machine is designed to grow through upgrades to more than 50 logical qubits.

Power management giant Eaton is now a customer, using private cloud access to Infleqtion’s machine to explore energy problems. And management said three paying customers—in finance, energy, and precision medicine—will run workloads on its logical-qubit demonstrations. On the Q2 call CEO Matt Kinsella said the computing business is coming in “a little hotter” than he expected.

In late September, Infleqtion announced it had created 30 entangled logical qubits using just 80 physical qubits on its Sqale quantum computer. That’s fewer than three physical qubits per logical qubit, well below the company’s own target of under 10.

But that headline needs some context. The code it used can detect errors, but it can’t correct most of them. The experiment threw out the runs where errors were caught. It’s real progress, but it’s not the same as the error correction that’s needed for a commercially useful machine.

There are three other things you should know.

First, Infleqtion’s $100 million CHIPS Act deal is still a letter of intent. D-Wave, Rigetti, and Quantinuum all finalized theirs in September. Infleqtion said in August it expects a final agreement later this year, but it hasn’t announced one as of this writing.

Second, its order book is thinner than its revenue might suggest. Backlog was about $21 million at the end of June. That’s much smaller than the other companies in the top 4, so Infleqtion must keep winning new contracts quickly to keep growing.

Third, the company restated its Q2 results just days after reporting them. The restatement moved some revenue on two government contracts out of 2024 and 2025 and into 2026. Second-quarter revenue went from $12.6 million to $13.5 million. The company called the change immaterial, but part of its latest guidance bump came from that accounting adjustment rather than new demand. It also filed its quarterly report a day late and disclosed “material weakness” in its internal controls. That’s not unusual for a frontier tech company that just went public through a SPAC. But it’s something to watch.

Bottom line: Infleqtion has more ways to win than anyone on this list (quantum computing, quantum sensing, and quantum software, which I didn’t talk about). But it needs to finalize the CHIPS deal. I also want to see the company publish a paper on its Sqale system and the 30 logical qubits it created with just 80 physical qubits.

Good morning @quipnetwork ☕️

I want to cover the quantum research result that I think is the single most important experimental finding for understanding the urgency of post-quantum security.

The 2023 IBM quantum error correction paper in Nature.

Not the Willow chip. Not the qubit count records. This specific paper. Here's why it changed how I think about the timeline.

The paper demonstrated a repetition code running on 127 physical qubits where the logical error rate decreased as the code distance increased.

That sentence requires unpacking because the implication is enormous.

Previous quantum error correction implementations shared a fundamental problem: as you added more qubits to improve error correction the overhead introduced new errors at roughly the same rate as the correction removed them. The net improvement was marginal. The scaling relationship was unfavorable.

The IBM Nature paper showed the relationship inverting.

More qubits. Better error correction. Net logical error rate going down as code distance goes up.

For the first time experimentally the error correction was winning against the noise.

Google's Willow result confirmed this a year later at larger scale and higher code distance. Two independent research groups. Two different hardware architectures. Same conclusion.

Quantum error correction scales favorably.

Here is the research implication stated as precisely as I can:

The engineering barrier that made fault-tolerant quantum computation seem perpetually 10 years away was the unfavorable scaling of error correction overhead. Every experimental result before 2023 suggested that noise grew faster than correction could compensate.

2023 and 2025 showed experimentally that this scaling relationship flips at sufficient code distance.

The barrier was real. Now it's been crossed. The path to fault-tolerant computation is open in a way it demonstrably was not before.

Shor's algorithm runs on fault-tolerant quantum hardware. The discrete logarithm problem the mathematical foundation of every wallet signature in crypto breaks on fault-tolerant quantum hardware.

The experimental confirmation that fault-tolerant scaling works changes the timeline from "theoretically possible but practically uncertain" to "engineering execution problem on a known trajectory."

Those are not the same thing.

My honest long view:

I read a lot of quantum research. Most results are incremental. Some are significant. A few are genuinely pivotal.

The favorable error correction scaling results from IBM and Google are pivotal. They are the experimental confirmation that the theoretical path to cryptographically relevant quantum computation is physically real rather than mathematically assumed.

Everything downstream of that confirmation @quipnetwork 's post-quantum wallets, the compute marketplace, the PoUW mechanism, the urgency of the airdrop window at https://t.co/5aKccd0qVp makes more sense when you understand what those papers actually proved.

The researchers updated their models in 2023. Most of CT hasn't updated theirs yet.
