Qubit counts alone can’t tell you how close quantum computers are to breaking encryption. The machine also has to correct its errors fast enough to finish the attack, and that depends partly on software running on ordinary computers.

Last week showed why:

Iceberg Quantum estimated RSA-2048 could be broken with 72,000 physical qubits in 3.7 days, assuming a 1µs correction cycle. Its decoder averages 4µs per round. How decoding keeps pace with that assumed cycle rate is an important implementation question.

Quantinuum reported an estimated logical-memory error rate of 5 × 10⁻⁶ per correction cycle, about five errors per million rounds. It decoded the experimental data offline. The same paper benchmarks decoders fast enough for real time, but the experiment didn’t use them live.

Leiden and Riverlane found standard correlated decoding erring about 4.4 times more often than simpler matching in one tested configuration with very low hardware error rates. They also proposed a fix.

When a smaller attack estimate makes headlines, check the conditions:

1. How reliable must the qubits be? Iceberg’s estimate assumes a physical error rate of roughly one in 1,000.
2. Has the complete error-correction system demonstrated the speed the estimate assumes?

Samsung's HBM revenue just passed SK hynix for the first time. At least, that's Bernstein's estimate: Q3 Samsung $8.7B vs SK hynix $7.6B.

Be clear on where that comes from. The report itself isn't public; I'm going off https://t.co/n6VSOfjT0S's and VLSI Korea's summaries. Bernstein back-calculated it from Korea's Jul–Sep HBM export data, and the Samsung figure actually came in ~10% below Bernstein's own earlier forecast.

On those numbers, Samsung grew +33% QoQ and SK hynix +11%. Both growing, Samsung much faster, on the HBM4 ramp. VLSI Korea cites Samsung's Q2 call: Q3 HBM4 revenue would be more than 3x the prior quarter.

But #1 in revenue isn't #1 at everything. Per reports cited by VLSI Korea, SK hynix is still the only one shipping 16-high HBM for Rubin in volume. The tallest stack is the hardest to build, and the easiest to sell.

Taiwan has a piece of this either way. SK hynix signed an MOU with TSMC (https://t.co/U2nKFTziDI / $TSM) in 2024: the HBM4 base die moves to TSMC logic process, and the HBM then goes into CoWoS alongside the GPU. Whoever sells the most HBM, the bottom of SK hynix's stack and the back-end packaging route through Taiwan.

So I'll wait for earnings: SK hynix Oct 28, Samsung Oct 29. If both disclose HBM revenue and HBM4 mix, we'll know whether Bernstein's number holds.

Not investment advice.

CSPs and AI labs: CSPs and AI labs had requested the development of lower-stack HBM products, such as 4-high and 6-high configurations, for use in low-end inference products. Those plans now appear to have been shelved, with 8-high once again emerging as the minimum stack height.

NVIDIA: Rubin’s specifications have changed amid base die supply constraints and requests from customers prioritizing bandwidth over cost efficiency. The original plan called for a mix of 8-high and 12-high HBM, but the 8-high option appears to have been dropped. For Rubin Ultra, scheduled for release in 2027, multiple architectural variants are currently undergoing tape-out. Initial versions are expected to use the highest-specification 8-high HBM4, while subsequent versions are expected to adopt either 8-high or 12-high HBM4E.

AMD: AMD is expected to use a mix of 8-high and 12-high HBM4 in its 2027 products. One notable development is the upcoming MI450, which is expected to increase the number of HBM stacks within the CoWoS package to 12, delivering 288GB of HBM4. The increase from eight to 12 HBM stacks per CoWoS package is a positive development for HBM content over the medium to long term.

OpenAI and Anthropic: OpenAI is expected to adopt 12-high HBM4, while Anthropic is expected to use 8-high HBM4.

Semiconductor substrates could become an even bigger bottleneck than electricity for AI. 

Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis, recently explained that semiconductor substrates could become an even bigger constraint on AI infrastructure expansion through 2027 and 2028 than electricity. He believes substrates and advanced PCB materials are the biggest bottleneck, followed by memory and optical components. For those unfamiliar, substrates are essentially the foundation that connects semiconductor chips to the rest of the system. As AI chips become larger and more complex, particularly with advanced packaging and multiple HBM stacks, manufacturing these substrates becomes increasingly difficult.

A lot of the critical suppliers are based in Japan, where companies have historically been conservative about expanding manufacturing capacity. So even if NVIDIA and other chipmakers continue increasing production, they could run into a situation where there simply aren't enough substrates to package those chips. This is also why NVIDIA recently announced agreements to expand substrate manufacturing capacity by 2.5x over the next three years, working with companies like Ibiden, Unimicron, and Samsung Electro-Mechanics. From an investing perspective, the companies I'm watching are Ibiden, Unimicron, Samsung Electro Mechanics, Ajinomoto, Nan Ya PCB, and Kinsus. Ajinomoto is particularly interesting because it supplies ABF insulating film, a critical material used in advanced semiconductor substrates, and has historically dominated that market.

I've talked extensively about memory, photonics, and power being some of my highest conviction areas in AI infrastructure, but I think substrates deserve a lot more research as well. If demand continues outpacing manufacturing capacity, the companies supplying these materials could be in a very favorable position over the next few years.
